name: Southern Coastal Yuin
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Besold, Jutta. 2012 [revised 2013]. Language Recovery of the New South Wales South Coast Aboriginal Languages. Part A: Analysis and Philology. PhD thesis, Australian National University. hdl:1885/10133 (ANU Open Research; opened). Secondary, carried: Eades, Diana K. 1976. The Dharawal and Dhurga Languages of the New South Wales South Coast. Australian Aboriginal Studies, Research and Regional Studies 8. Canberra: AIAS, p.25 (StressTyp2 878, entry 'Dhurga; Thaua'; book unreached).
catalog_locator: Besold 2012 Part A, sec. A.3.5 'Stress' pp.112-115; A.3.5.1 'Stress pattern' pp.113-115. Eades 1976:25 = StressTyp2 entry 878 ('Dhurga; Thaua')
catalog_quote: The general stress pattern in SCLs is commonly observed in AALs (Dixon, 2002a:557). Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words and no example is found in the source material that shows stress on the final syllable in a disyllabic word. Words that are still used in communities are often pronounced with stress on a long vowel on the final syllable. For example, Mathews transcribed budjan ‘bird’ <boo'-jan> (U-M.1.1) and miriga <mir'-re-ka> (DW-M.2.2-27), clearly marking stress on the first syllable, whereas some speakers in communities pronounce both words with a long vowel and stress on the second/final syllable. ... In words with three syllables or more, primary stress falls on the first or second syllable. Where stress is marked on a second syllable in a polysyllabic word, a long vowel in that stressed syllable is in some cases indicated. ... It is possible that collectors may have misinterpreted long vowel pronunciation as stress on that syllable. ... But Mathews also transcribed words that show that stress and vowel length are independent. Both examples show stress marked on the first syllable, but long vowel on second, or third, syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Philologically reconstituted from Mathews', Howitt's and Tindale's stress marks for the NSW South Coast languages as a group (Dharrawal, Dharumba, Dhurga, Djirringanj, with a Dhaawa/Thawa item cited): primary stress is word-initial in disyllables (never final); in words of three or more syllables it is on the first or, in some items, the second syllable, second-syllable stress often coinciding with a transcribed long vowel (Besold allows that Mathews may have marked length rather than stress there); stress and vowel length are otherwise independent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (only 'primary stress' in polysyllables is mentioned; no statement on secondary/rhythmic stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Second-syllable stress in some trisyllabic+ words, usually with a long vowel (e.g. burnaaga 'goanna' <bur-nâ'-ga> Mathews vs <'bana:ga> Tindale); collectors sometimes disagree on the same word; present-day community pronunciations of some words (budjan 'bird', miriga) shift stress to a lengthened final/second vowel; one Mathews text note 'yuinbuloalā (the accent on the last syllable)' for yuwinj-bulawala 'many men' (Part B ex. 51).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress inferred from stress diacritics on isolated citation forms in 19th/early-20th-century wordlists and notebooks (no living L1 speakers; no acoustic data). Statement is made for the 'SCLs' collectively, not for Thawa/Dhaawa alone, whose corpus Besold says is limited to wordlists; the evidence cited includes Djirringanj (DJ-AH.1.3 <ma'bra>) and Dhaawa (DW-M.2.2-27 <mir'-re-ka>) items, both constituents of Glottolog's Southern Coastal Yuin.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's 'Southern Coastal Yuin' [sout2771, ISO xtv 'Thawa'] corresponds to the Southern Coastal cell of Wafer & Lissarrague's (2008:105) Yuin dialect cycle = Djirringanj (Dyirringany, Bega/Wallaga Lake area) + Dhaawa/Thawa/Thaua (Twofold Bay); it is a sister of Dhurga [dhur1239] and Thurawal [thur1254]. Besold's stress statement is made for the NSW 'South Coast languages' as a group (Dharrawal thur1254, Dharumba, Dhurga dhur1239, Djirringanj), explicitly citing a Djirringanj item (Howitt <ma'bra>) and a Dhaawa item (Mathews <mir'-re-ka>, DW-M.2.2-27); Besold states the Dhaawa corpus itself is only wordlists. No Thawa-specific phonology exists; the languages have had no L1 speakers since the early 20th century and the evidence is philological (collectors' stress marks), not acoustic.
